title: Bandwidth-aware layer-splitting for multi-GPU inference (draft)
content:
Summary:

This is an exploratory design note for a bandwidth-aware layer-splitting strategy to improve latency and tail stability for multi-GPU inference serving. The goal: blend light-weight pipeline slicing with interconnect/topology-aware layer placement and NCCL tuning to minimize cross-GPU round trips for KV cache and activation exchange while preserving memory headroom for large-context KV caching. This doc is intentionally experimental — contains ideas, measurement proposals, and potential rollout steps.

Motivation / problem statement:

- Many inference workloads are in the regime where single-request latency matters (chat, tool-calling) and the model size forces us to span multiple accelerators.
- Traditional pipeline-parallel shards and pure tensor-parallel strategies each have tradeoffs: pipeline cuts reduce per-device memory but add sequential hops (higher latency), tensor parallelism reduces hops but increases NCCL allreduce overhead and can hurt KV cache locality.
- Existing sharding heuristics are model-agnostic and ignore PCIe/NVLink topology and observed layer communication patterns. That leads to unnecessary cross-socket traffic and volatile tail latency.

Design idea (high level):

1) Profile-driven layer affinity: at model onboarding, run a lightweight analyzer that estimates per-layer activation size, KV lifetime, and per-token cross-layer bandwidth. Compute an affinity score for grouping contiguous layers that minimize inter-device activation exchange given the cluster interconnect matrix.

2) Bandwidth-aware split points: instead of evenly slicing by parameter count, allow split points at layer boundaries chosen to (a) balance memory, (b) localize KV cache segments to GPUs that have high-bandwidth links to the majority of requester-connections, and (c) minimize peak inter-GPU bandwidth per timestep.

3) Hybrid micro-pipeline within a request: for short tokens or low-latency SLOs, place critical early layers on a low-latency GPU and move later layers to a bandwidth-rich backplane. We micro-schedule so some requests are served mostly on the front-device (less hops) while larger-context requests may use distributed stages.

4) Interconnect topology-aware NCCL config: pick collective algorithms dynamically per-collective and per-job. For NVLink-heavy groups, enable ring algorithms with larger chunk sizes; for mixed NVLink/PCIe groups use tree/hierarchical collectives with manual chunking. Provide a per-placement NCCL profile that sets NCCL_ALGO and chunk sizes.

5) KV cache placement & routing: shard KV cache by prefix-sharding heuristic (recent prefixes grouped together) and colocate hot prefixes with lower-latency frontend GPUs. Maintain a compact routing table for fast remap on failover. Cache migration should be incremental (chunked) and scheduled during low-util windows or pre-warmed via background transfer.

Operational primitives required:

- Interconnect matrix collector: runtime agent that queries topology (NVLink groups, PCIe switch hops, GPU-to-GPU bandwidth) and exposes a numeric affinity matrix used during placement.
- Layer profiler: offline tool that runs microbenchmarks on a representative input length distribution and reports per-layer activation size and KV read/write ratio.
- Placement optimizer: greedy (fast path) plus ILP fallback (slow path) that consumes device memory budgets, affinity matrix, per-layer cost to output shard boundaries.
- NCCL policy manager: maps placement -> NCCL env + chunking parameters; can be overridden for A/B testing.
- KV routing service: small metadata plane that maps request-prefix -> shard owner GPU and supports atomic remap + background sync.

Tradeoffs and risks:

- Complexity: adds onboarding cost and more moving parts that can fail (placement optimizer, routing plane). We must keep a conservative default that falls back to current strategies.
- Migration tail: moving large KV shards can create network storms; need rate-limited background sync and throttled cutover.
- Model diversity: models with non-uniform layer compute (e.g., Mixture-of-Experts) might defeat simple heuristics; require model-specific overrides.

Microbenchmarks / experiments to validate:

1) Synthetic layer shapes: synthesize 3 model shapes — uniform layers, front-heavy (early layers bigger), back-heavy — and measure 50/95/99 latencies under 200/400/800-token contexts across three cluster topologies (NVLink line, NVLink ring, PCIe only).

Metrics: tail latency, per-hop bandwidth, GPU utilization, KV miss rate, background migrate bandwidth.

2) NCCL algorithm ablation: for same placement, sweep NCCL_ALGO=ring,tree,collnet with multiple chunk sizes and measure time for AllGather/AllReduce calls in the serving-critical path. Report difference in per-token overhead and memory usage.

3) KV-shard placement heatmap: track hot prefixes across a 24h workload trace; evaluate a simple LRU prefix coalescing and measure hit rate improvement when colocating hot prefixes vs round-robin.

Implementation plan (rough phases):

Phase 0 — lab-only prototypes (2-4 weeks)
- Build layer profiler and interconnect matrix collector.
- Implement simple greedy placement (balance memory, minimize estimated cross-host bytes).
- Run microbenchmarks and collect baseline numbers.

Phase 1 — internal canary (4-6 weeks)
- Integrate NCCL policy manager. Add per-deployment feature flag.
- Implement KV routing metadata plane with in-memory store and background sync.
- Canary on internal workloads (non-prod) with explicit fallback to single-GPU or existing multi-GPU policy.

Phase 2 — customer pilot (6-12 weeks)
- Add migration throttles, graceful fallback on partial failures.
- Expose telemetry (per-request hops, NCCL algo, per-shard KV hit).
- Pilot with 1–2 customers on Dedicated clusters.

Phase 3 — GA and defaults (ongoing)
- Harden placement optimizer, add pre-warm migration heuristics.
- Automated rollback and safety checks.

Compatibility and safety concerns:

- Security: KV cache migration must not leak tenant data. Any background transfer needs encryption over RDMA/NVLink if applicable, and be constrained by tenant isolation rules.
- Determinism: Ensure deterministic routing table updates in multi-controller setups. Use leader election and sequenced ops.
- Debuggability: expose verbose tracing for hops, collectives, and KV remap events; provide a simulator to reproduce placement decisions.

Observability / metrics to add:

- per-request hop_count (int)
- per-collective latency + bytes transferred (tags: algo, chunk_size)
- KV_shard_hit_rate_by_prefix (histogram)
- migration_background_bytes/sec (gauge)
- placement_recalc_count and reason (scale event, model onboard, manual)

Rollout safety checklist (minimal):

- Canary default disabled in control plane.
- Per-tenant opt-in flag.
- Auto-fallback: if per-request tail increases beyond X% for 10m, revert to previous placement.
- Migration bandwidth cap default 100 MB/s per GPU.
- Dry-run mode to output placement proposals without executing migration.

Open questions / TODOs (short):

- How to handle heterogeneous GPU memory sizes in same cluster (A100 40GB + 80GB)? Greedy placement needs to respect fragmentation.
- Heuristic for prefix grouping: time-window-based vs workload-aware (session affinity).
- When is tensor-parallel preferable to pipeline split for extremely wide layers? Need threshold formula.
- Investigate NVLink peer-bw asymmetry for multi-socket nodes; how to encode in affinity matrix.

Notes to self / links:

- See perf traces in github.com/redwood-inference/perf/kv-bandwidth-experiments (WIP).
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime: "nccl-topology-experiments" (search id 6743).
- Related doc: "slice-and-stitch-multi-gpu-playbook" — overlapping concerns but different approach (this doc focuses on bandwidth-awareness and KV-locality).

Appendix: short example placement output (dry-run) for 24-layer transformer, two nodes (4 GPUs each):

- Proposed splits: layers 0-6 -> GPU0 (nodeA), layers 7-13 -> GPU1 (nodeA), layers 14-18 -> GPU2 (nodeB), layers 19-23 -> GPU3 (nodeB)
- Rationale: early layers small activations colocated on NVLink pair with frontend NIC; mid layers heavier placed on NVLink ring low-latency; late layers largest activations grouped on nodeB where PCIe bandwidth is higher to disk-backed KV prefetch.
- NCCL profile: intra-node ring chunk_size=4MB, inter-node collectives use tree with chunk_size=1MB and COLLNET disabled.

If you want I can:
- add a synthetic benchmark runner and sample scripts;
- sketch the placement optimizer pseudo-code;
- start a small canary PR that wires up NCCL env toggles per-deployment.

Tagged owners for follow-up: @Ethan Cole (profiling harness), @Ravi Anand (NCCL policy), @Marisol Vega (KV routing).

End of draft.
